section_summary: This section consists chiefly of FBI cover letters and investigative memoranda sent to the Department of State concerning Japanese organizations, commercial networks, propaganda, clandestine correspondence, and suspected espionage in Mexico and South America during 1944–45. Major subjects include the Kyoeikai mutual-aid organization in Mexico; linked Japanese trading companies and suspected communications networks in Brazil, Argentina, Chile, and Peru; Japanese representatives working through the Spanish Embassy in Lima; and investigations of individuals suspected of assisting Japanese intelligence. The section also contains correspondence about Japanese publications, a bibliography on Japan, and the transmission and acknowledgment of an FBI monograph titled “The Japanese in Latin America.”

subfiles.title: Japanese Publications
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports efforts to obtain four Japanese publications in Portuguese for the Department of State.
subfiles.summary: Hoover replies to a State Department request of December 23, 1944. He states that steps have already been taken to procure Japanese publications numbered 22, 26, 30, and 32 and promises to forward them upon their arrival in Washington.

subfiles.title: Comité Japonés de Ayuda Mutua, also known as Comité Japonés de Auxilio Mutuo, “Kyoeikai” — Mexico
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits background information on the Japanese mutual-aid organization Kyoeikai in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The letter describes the Kyoeikai as an ostensible relief society for Japanese removed from strategic areas and resettled elsewhere in Mexico. It identifies Luis Tadasu Tsuji, Guillermo S. Makita, and Kiso Tsuru as leading figures and notes communal farming projects in Morelos and a subcommittee in Guadalajara. Hoover states that the information was also supplied to the U.S. Embassy and military and naval attachés in Mexico.

subfiles.title: Background Memorandum on the Kyoeikai in Mexico
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Details the personnel, finances, agricultural colonies, relief work, and government supervision of the Kyoeikai in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies the Kyoeikai’s officers, associated Japanese nationals, and plans for cooperative farms organized through Mexico City and Guadalajara. It describes Hacienda Castro Urdiales and a larger communal colony near Cuernavaca, including their capitalization, management, and intended support for displaced Japanese families. Much of the report examines disputed attempts to obtain frozen Japanese commercial and legation funds, as well as fundraising within the Japanese colony. It concludes with information about the Guadalajara subcommittee and Mexican government surveillance of the organization’s meetings and agricultural activities.

subfiles.title: Japanese Publications
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards original Japanese-language copies of four publications after Portuguese editions proved unavailable.
subfiles.summary: Hoover reports that Portuguese versions of publications 22, 26, 30, and 32 can no longer be obtained. The FBI instead transmits the original Japanese texts: “A Study of Laws for Economy in Time of War,” “History of War,” “Album of Sino-Japanese War,” and “Rural and Youth Questions.” The Department is asked to return the books after use.

subfiles.title: Return of Japanese Publications to the Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.to: Federal Bureau of Investigation, attention Ralph R. Roach
subfiles.about: Returns four Japanese publications loaned to the Department of State.
subfiles.summary: The Department returns the package of four publications transmitted under the FBI memorandum of January 25, 1945. It repeats the titles and notes that the Bureau had requested their return as soon as they had served their purpose.

subfiles.title: List of Books Relating to Japan
subfiles.about: Lists English-language books on modern Japanese history, society, government, nationalism, and expansion.
subfiles.summary: The bibliography contains thirteen books published between 1918 and 1943. Its subjects include Japanese government, Shinto nationalism, population, military rule, cultural history, and policy conflict in the Pacific and Far East.

subfiles.title: Japanese Nationals Operating in South America
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits an investigative memorandum on Japanese nationals suspected of espionage and commercial activity in South America.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards a memorandum dated December 27, 1944, from a confidential source. He characterizes the case as involving a large group of Japanese nationals believed to be serving the Japanese government throughout South America for espionage and commercial purposes. The information was also made available to the U.S. Embassy in Rio de Janeiro.

subfiles.title: Ryokichi Nagai; Suetaka Hayao; Dr. Alberto Goes Telles; et al.
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Investigates suspicious correspondence linking Japanese commercial firms and individuals in Rio de Janeiro, Buenos Aires, and Santiago.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum analyzes letters addressed through Brazilian lawyers Alberto Goes Telles and Ary P. de Andrade Figueira for Ryokichi Nagai and Suetaka Hayao, including an undecoded message and instructions designed to conceal correspondence. It links Sociedade Comercial Nipo-Brasileira with the Nambei company in Buenos Aires and Sociedad Comercial Chilena Oriental in Santiago, firms suspected of channeling intelligence to Japan. Later correspondence concerns the Brazilian liquidation of the Rio company, Nagai’s finances, and remittances routed through Telles and the Red Cross. Investigators found Telles evasive and noted contradictions between his statements and documentary evidence of his earlier role as an intermediary.

subfiles.title: Masuro Okamoto (Yokoyama), with Aliases
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a memorandum on the Japanese-affairs secretary at the Spanish Embassy in Lima.
subfiles.summary: Hoover identifies Masuro Okamoto as the recently appointed secretary for Japanese affairs at the Spanish Embassy in Lima. Okamoto succeeded Victor Tateishi, who had been deported from Peru for internment in the United States. The attached report summarizes information from a reliable confidential source.

subfiles.title: Masuro Okamoto (Yokoyama), Alias Luis Okamoto, Masaro Yokoyama, Masuru Okamoto
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Examines Okamoto’s Embassy duties, community connections, aliases, family, and alleged role in Japanese nationalist networks in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum recounts Victor Tateishi’s deportation and the Spanish Embassy’s successful request to employ Peruvian-born Masuro Okamoto as his replacement. It describes the Embassy’s Japanese-affairs work, including pensions, alien-registration renewals, voluntary deportation, remittances, complaints, and supervision of deportees’ property. Sources alleged that older Japanese leaders—especially Yoshiyuki Tamura—actually directed Okamoto and connected him with a Japanese youth organization and Yoshitaro Amano. The report also discusses suspicious family correspondence and an uncorroborated allegation concerning Isabel Okada’s frozen funds, then supplies a physical and biographical description of Okamoto.

subfiles.title: Japanese in Peru Connected with Choko Shirakawa
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a detailed memorandum on Japanese residents of Peru in contact with Choko Shirakawa in Buenos Aires.
subfiles.summary: The letter forwards information from a reliable confidential source concerning Japanese residents of Peru who corresponded with Choko Shirakawa, an employee of Japanese interests in Buenos Aires. Hoover notes that the information was available to the U.S. embassies in Buenos Aires, La Paz, Santiago, and Lima.

subfiles.title: Choko Shirakawa et al. — Lima, Peru
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Investigates a coded correspondence system operating through Sociedad Anónima Taibo and associated Japanese commercial personnel in Peru, Chile, and Argentina.
subfiles.summary: The investigation began after coded letters from Peru and Chile were sent to Choko Shirakawa through the cover name Juan Roberto Martinez in Buenos Aires. The report reconstructs Sociedad Anónima Taibo’s origins in Pacific Trading Company, including a failed prewar attempt to purchase Peruvian oil fields for supplying Japan, and profiles its partners and managers. Interrogations of Bunji Oashi and Juan Barthelmes revealed that Taibo addresses served as mail drops and that Yoshitomo Yamamoto encoded communications routed among Lima, Santiago, and Buenos Aires, allegedly under instructions from former attaché Shinichi Yokoyama. The memorandum also profiles Yamamoto, Hideo Ando, Iwao Takenaka, and the commercial and nationalist activities surrounding the network.

subfiles.title: Tomiya Koseki; Japanese Activities in Chile and Argentina
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards additional information about Carlos Santa Cruz and Luz Poblete in connection with Tomiya Koseki.
subfiles.summary: Hoover refers to an earlier April 24 report on Tomiya Koseki and encloses new information about Carlos Santa Cruz and Luz Poblete. The report was supplied to the U.S. embassies in Buenos Aires and Santiago.

subfiles.title: Tomiya Koseki, with Aliases, et al. — Santiago, Chile
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Reports allegations that Luz Poblete acted as a Japanese courier and discussed a failed plan to send saboteurs to the United States.
subfiles.summary: An informant stated that Luz Poblete and her son Carlos Santa Cruz were strongly pro-Axis and that she served as a courier between Chile and Argentina for Japanese interests. Poblete allegedly said that approximately twenty individuals, including her son, were to enter the United States as students or tourists and sabotage war industries, but that the plan failed because they could not obtain passage. The informant lacked documentary proof or further definite information about her espionage role.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities in South America
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits information concerning Japanese agents in Argentina, Chile, and Peru.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards a memorandum based on a confidential and reliable source regarding Japanese agents in three South American countries. He states that the material was also available to the U.S. embassies in Buenos Aires, Lima, and Santiago.

subfiles.title: Choko Shirakawa et al. — Santiago, Chile
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Identifies Santiago Taibo personnel linked to the clandestine correspondence network uncovered in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Following the interrogation of Juan Barthelmes and Bunji Oashi, investigators identified “Huyamura” as likely Yadaharu Uyemura and “Kawaguchi” as Kenosuke Kawaguchi, both associated with Casa Taibo in Chile. The report supplies police-registration information for Uyemura and describes Kawaguchi as Casa Taibo’s president, the son of the Pacific Trading Company president, and a writer of business reports for the Japanese Legation. It closes by noting another Japanese agent whose name is poorly preserved in the OCR and who appeared in intercepted 1943 espionage messages.

subfiles.title: Alfonso Letelier (Llona), Alias Alfred Letelier — Chile
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits an investigation of Alfonso Letelier after his name was found in Yoshitaro Amano’s notebook.
subfiles.summary: Hoover notes that Letelier and alleged Japanese intelligence chief Yoshitaro Amano traveled from Valparaíso toward the Canal Zone on the same ship. The investigation, however, found Letelier to be pro-Allied and uncovered no evidence connecting him to Japanese subversive activity. The information was supplied to the U.S. Embassy in Santiago.

subfiles.title: Alfonso Letelier (Llona), Alias Alfred Letelier — Santiago, Chile
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Assesses Alfonso Letelier’s background and his incidental contact with Yoshitaro Amano during a 1938 voyage.
subfiles.summary: The report traces Letelier’s family, education, profession as an agricultural engineer and composer, travel, and pro-Allied political reputation. Letelier explained that he met an unidentified Japanese passenger, probably Yoshitaro Amano, aboard a 1938 voyage from Valparaíso and conversed with him casually about tourist photographs, one of which showed the Letelier family farm. Passenger records confirmed that Letelier and Amano were aboard the SS Santa Barbara, although Amano left at Balboa while Letelier continued to New York. Investigators found no later contact or evidence of subversive activity.

subfiles.title: Transmission of “The Japanese in Latin America” to Frederick B. Lyon
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Sends Lyon a copy of the FBI monograph “The Japanese in Latin America.”
subfiles.summary: Hoover transmits a monograph compiled mainly from reports by confidential and reliable sources. He notes that copies were also provided to Secretary of State James F. Byrnes and Assistant Secretary of State Spruille Braden.

subfiles.title: Transmission of “The Japanese in Latin America” to Spruille Braden
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Spruille Braden, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Sends Braden a copy of the FBI monograph “The Japanese in Latin America.”
subfiles.summary: Hoover states that the enclosed monograph was prepared chiefly from reports received from confidential and reliable sources. The letter is the formal transmittal of the study to the Assistant Secretary of State.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of “The Japanese in Latin America”
subfiles.from: Spruille Braden, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the FBI monograph “The Japanese in Latin America.”
subfiles.summary: Braden thanks Hoover for his December 26 letter and the enclosed FBI monograph. He states that he is glad to have the study and appreciates Hoover’s sending it.
